articles.title: Men have used wealth and fame to get away with abuse. No longer | Andy Burnham
articles.description: The NDAs that enforce silence, the behaviour that exploits the age of consent. I'll address both with sweeping changes to keep women and girls safe Burnham opens door to wider NDAs ban at ‘watershed moment’ on abuse Powerful men using their fame and money to silence anyone who calls out their behaviour. Victims treated as though they’re the ones who’ve done something wrong. And a culture where abuse can hide in plain sight because people in positions of power think they can get away with it. articles.author: Nick Ames at the Etihad Stadium
articles.title: Rayan Cherki magic denies Napoli but Manchester City’s struggles continue
articles.description: For reasons best known to those eyeing the pound signs, Manchester City gave a debut to a special rust-coloured kit in front of a nonplussed crowd. It was of a piece with their performance for most of a familiarly frustrating night that at least concluded with a shot of energy, the home side belatedly shaking off their torpor and ending the prospect of a triumphant return to the Etihad for Kevin De Bruyne. Despite the relief sparked by a fine equaliser by Rayan Cherki, who was rewarded for an insistent but hitherto fruitless evening’s endeavours when his angled shot flashed past Vanja Milinkovic-Savic, it was hard to see this as anything but a perfect snapshot of their autumn difficulties. Nobody could pretend City were up against crack opposition in a one-paced Napoli, who are eighth in Serie A and lack the brio of old, but they simply cannot keep the door shut and could not have quibbled about departing with a defeat. articles.title: Dortmund’s Beier halts Arsenal charge after thunderbolt from Gyökeres
articles.description: Arsenal’s sky-high standards are slipping. For the second time in four days, Mikel Arteta’s side found themselves a goal up at half-time and apparently coasting toward victory, only for their opponents to rouse themselves and earn a deserved draw. After Newcastle on Saturday , this time it was an impressive Borussia Dortmund who became only the second side to take points off Arsenal in their past 15 group stage games in this competition. It could have been worse had an offside flag not ruled out Jobe ­Bellingham’s goal after Max Beier equalised a thunderbolt from Viktor Gyökeres. But the much-maligned Sweden striker was guilty of a glaring miss late on as Arsenal laid siege to Dortmund’s goal, racking up 30 shots by the final whistle. The German side had to hang on for a result that gave their travelling fans a night to remember, although Arteta admitted his players must be more clinical when Real Madrid and Jude Bellingham visit north London in a fortnight. articles.author: Editorial
articles.title: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
articles.description: Ministers have taken on board their MPs’ message about cuts. Now anxious claimants need reassurance Four million people with disabilities or long‑term health conditions in the UK claim personal independence payment (Pip). A review by Sir Stephen Timms, the social security minister, offers a blueprint for how to overhaul it . Its recommendations pose a difficult question for ministers: are they prepared to meet the needs that a more accurate assessment of the costs of disability might reveal? Sir Stephen worked as one of three co-chairs with a steering group of 12 people with a range of professional and lived experience. There is broad agreement that Pip needs to be reformed. The announcement on Tuesday that the government would accept the recommendation of a new fast track for claimants whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve, and abolish unnecessary benefit reviews, signalled that ministers are ready for change. The decision, affecting one in 10 claimants in England and Wales, is welcome but long overdue. Ministers should work with the devolved administrations to ensure similar progress elsewhere in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham and Wales: a devolution blindspot at No 10 | Editorial
articles.description: The PM has summarily dismissed Welsh demands for further powers similar to those enjoyed in Scotland. The approach seems at odds with his consensual style As he headed for Downing Street this summer, Andy Burnham said that he aimed to be “as collaborative and pragmatic as possible” in his dealings with the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. His predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, had notoriously warned ministers against being “overly deferential” in discussions with the devolved administrations. But Mr Burnham’s signature commitment to distributing more power and responsibility out of Westminster, and his consensual style, appeared to augur well for a positive reset in relations. In Wales, this early optimism has just been brutally quashed by an uncharacteristically peremptory letter from Mr Burnham to the first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth. In it, the prime minister flatly rejected Welsh calls for the devolving of powers in relation to policing and justice, the crown estate and rail infrastructure. In the case of policing, Mr Burnham is in the curious position of denying to Mr ap Iorwerth the type of power that he enjoyed as the mayor of Greater Manchester. articles.description: The former Labour prime minister is wrong to dismiss all zero-sum thinking as misguided, writes Gavin Bailey The broad thrust of Gordon Brown’s argument is correct ( The far right is menacing Europe – but it is fragile. What the extremists and voters want isn’t the same, 22 November ). However, he is wrong to suggest that zero-sum beliefs are erroneous. Many things in life are zero-sum. If I own a house, you can’t also own it; if I burn some gas to heat it, you can’t use the same gas. If the UK makes all the cars for the European market, other countries’ carmakers won’t be making them. Yes, growth can come from collaboration and trade, but the proceeds are not infinite and take time to achieve. Continue reading...

articles.title: Why white-tailed sea eagles are a danger to Britain’s seabirds | Letters
articles.description: The reintroduction of the birds in England and Wales spells disaster for fragile marine ecosystems, warns Tim Birkhead Your article on white-tailed sea eagle reintroduction ( Reintroduction of white-tailed eagles puts seabird colonies at risk of wipeout, say experts, 8 November ) highlighted the risk that white-tailed sea eagles are likely to pose to Britain’s seabirds. To argue, as Prof Ian Convery and Rebecca Wrigley did in their responses ( Letters, 15 November ), that the re-establishment of white-tailed sea eagles will somehow restore a lost paradise is fallacious. Where is the evidence that sea eagles will restore that balance? There is no evidence. Also, suggesting that because in the distant past sea eagles and seabirds coexisted, their reintroduction will pose no problems is naive. By failing to acknowledge that past marine ecosystems were much more robust, and seabird prey more abundant, than they are today, these two authors miss the point that it is precisely because our seabirds are currently short of food that they are so vulnerable to disturbance and predation from white-tailed sea eagles. Continue reading...

articles.description: Reform leader is happy to return to his anti-EU happy place, where the truth can be whatever you want it to be This feels like Nigel Farage’s happy place. articles.title: Mariella Frostrup calls AJ Odudu ‘aggressive’ – and here we go again. We tire of this angry black woman trope | Natalie Morris
articles.description: Microaggressions pile up, and then they are triggering. Amid the latest row on I’m a Celebrity, we’re obliged to explain this hurt all over again When I heard Mariella Frostrup call AJ Odudu “aggressive” over the weekend on I’m a Celebrity … Get Me Out of Here!, my heart sank with sick recognition. For her part, AJ’s mother has since said that watching her daughter experience this all-too-familiar dynamic was a “living hell”. I know many Black women tuning in will have felt a collective shudder of disgust and solidarity. Of course, there is pushback. “Our addiction to offence is tearing us apart,” wrote a Telegraph pundit on Monday . But, this language is not neutral. There is a long history of Black women having their conduct and tone disproportionately scrutinised by white people. And what happened between Odudu and Frostrup is a tale as old as time. A Black woman stands up for herself and, no matter how reasonably she presents her argument, she is accused of aggression. It is an efficient tactic to flip the focus on to the behaviour of the Black woman, and it is rooted in racist stereotypes. Natalie Morris is the author of Mixed/Other: Explorations of Multiraciality in Modern Britain Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment
articles.description: A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point. With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom. Continue reading...

articles.description: A professor at the age of 21, Christopher Dresser was a design genius who created beautiful, futuristic homeware, from teapots to toast racks to jugs. As a child, he was so artistically gifted he went to design school in 1847 when he was just 13. He became a professor at 21, dreaming up theories based on plant structure that changed the way designers worked. But it was after he quit academia that he really started to break boundaries. As a self-declared “design doctor”, he experimented with production techniques that brought beautiful, futuristic homeware into everyday houses. He was one of the first western designers to travel to Japan, helping introduce Japonisme to British life, which has had a transformative effect on furniture and decoration ever since. articles.author: Geoffrey Robertson
articles.title: Why the genocide verdict against Myanmar has big implications for Israel | Geoffrey Robertson
articles.description: Proving the ‘crime of crimes’ against an individual is notoriously difficult, but the ICJ has set a precedent for states to be found liable. Israel could be next For the first time ever, a state has been found guilty of genocide – that “crime of crimes” – and has been ordered to compensate victims and to prosecute and punish the perpetrators. This judgment came from the international court of justice (ICJ), which has convicted Myanmar of killing and expelling many thousands of Rohingyas in Rakhine state in 2017 . The court did not change the definition of the crime, settled by the genocide convention in 1948 as requiring proof of an intention to destroy, in whole or part, a racial or religious group as such. But it made the prospect of proving this against a nation a good deal easier than against an individual. It set a precedent for its next case concerning state liability, namely the case brought by South Africa against Israel. Geoffrey Robertson KC was a UN appeal judge and is author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? articles.title: Outcry grows over Labour plan to exempt most brownfield sites from nature protection rules
articles.description: Chancellor’s decision to exempt plots up to 1.5 hectares allows developers to dodge rules aiming to reverse wildlife declines An outcry is growing over the UK chancellor’s removal of most brownfield housing plots from a legal requirement for developers to measurably enhance nature. John Healey’s decision in the budget to exempt brownfield plots of up to 1.5 hectares from biodiversity net gain (BNG) laws effectively means housing developers of inner-city, urban and surburban sites will be able to dodge rules designed to reverse steep wildlife declines while also allowing housebuilding growth. According to government data, 86% of brownfield sites currently registered are 1.5ha or under. Continue reading...

articles.author: Andrew Cordon
articles.title: Scream 4 came out 15 years ago – but its mockery of online brainrot is more spot-on than ever
articles.description: When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit . It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did. Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4. articles.author: Charlotte Jansen
articles.title: What happened when the man who took a million photographs embraced colour?
articles.description: The Photographers’ Gallery, London Sanlé Sory is known for his black and white images taken during independence in Burkina Faso – but his colour portraits bring humour, insouciance and joy Despite his wide renown, there have been hardly any major exhibitions of Sanlé Sory’s work. His last UK show was in 2019, concentrating on the black-and-white images the Burkinabé photographer made in the first two decades after opening his own studio, Volta Photo, in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960 – a period that coincided with the first two decades of independence in Burkina Faso. This new Photographer’s Gallery show shifts the focus to the 1980s and 1990s, when Sory began working in colour. It’s easy to see why, even with few exhibitions, Sory has made such an impression on audiences. There are the familiar west African studio photography tropes westerners love, where sound, image, fashion and pose collide. The props are popping, the style is irrepressible, the energy is irresistible. I wonder if Sory’s speed and instinct came from the time he spent early in his career racing on his motorbike to photograph car accidents for newspapers and the police. These portraits are the opposite of a car crash, they’re remedially joyful, wilfully alive – but they share that feeling of being inside the moment, at the edge of something. Continue reading...

articles.author: Michael Hogan
articles.title: ‘The icing on the cake’: how Nigella saved Bake Off
articles.description: Viewing figures are up and the new judge has spiced up the show with her wit, charm and articulate appreciation of doughy delights. The stale previous seasons are fast becoming a mere memory When Nigella Lawson helps crown the new champion of The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday night, two other winners will also be celebrating: the show itself and broadcaster Channel 4. The fabled “Nigella effect” has freshened up a franchise that was beginning to taste distinctly stale. Having replaced Prue Leith as judge for this 17th edition, alongside the ever-present Paul Hollywood, the domestic goddess has made the cake-making contest essential viewing again. Prompting a public outpouring of love, magisterial Lawson has proved the missing ingredient in the show’s resurgence. Continue reading...

articles.author: Daniel Wolfe
articles.title: GTA VI’s jaw-dropping success: in figures
articles.description: Content creators have produced hundreds of millions of hours of video game since its launch Grand Theft Auto ( GTA) VI became the largest video game release of all time last week and while it is hard to say exactly how many people are playing the game (current estimates say at least 30 million), there are plenty of other jaw-dropping data points we do know. Data on streaming the game suggests that only two days into its release a cumulative 364.5m hours have been watched – roughly 41,000 years of content. Put another way, that translates to more than 41,000 years worth of people riffling through cash registers, hanging drywall, birding, diving or hijacking jets. That’s according to streaming data from Streams Charts, a data and analytics company that has been tracking Rockstar Game’s long-awaited title. Continue reading...

articles.author: Anna Berrill
articles.title: The secret to the perfect Christmas party cocktail
articles.description: Festive drinks are all about capturing the warmth and theatre of the season, so lean into wintry flavours such as orange and cloves, and add a bit of drama by bringing out the blowtorch What are the best cocktails to make for a Christmas party? Dan, by email We’re all in favour of getting the party season started early, Dan, so now is as good a time as any to get your drinks cupboard in order. “Ultimately, Christmas cocktails are all about bringing a little warmth, nostalgia and theatre, so don’t be afraid to have fun with seasonal flavours,” says Josie Pink, author of River Cottage: Cocktails and Botanicals . The smell of orange, be it fresh or dried, is never too far away at this time of year, and one reason Pink suggests having a batch of orange liquor on hand, not least “to rustle up a margarita or two”. Ditto dried citrus wheels: “They’re a must,” she says. “Not only are they gorgeous for adorning cocktails, but any misshapes can be turned into marmalade dust, and any spares into home decorations.” Pink also advises getting some syrups in your arsenal – “I’d opt for a batch of trusty vanilla syrup” – plus a chai number “for those fragrant, warming spice flavours that we all associate with the festive season”. If there’s a gang coming over, you’ll likely find Pink ladling hot mulled apple juice laced with citrussy gin into mugs, or making pitchers of rum punch: “Either would warm the cockles.” Alternatively, consider a “slightly lighter” mulled white wine: “Gently warm your favourite white wine with spices such as star anise, cinnamon, ginger and cloves, sweeten with syrup and citrus, then spike with apple cider brandy.” Got a culinary dilemma? articles.author: Alexandra Coghlan
articles.title: RPO/Hisaishi review – Studio Ghibli’s genius brings his concerto to a rapt London
articles.description: Royal Albert Hall, London The Royal Philharmonic rode the bucking rhythms of the star composer’s intricate score, the highlight of an evening that also included works by Steve Reich and David Lang If anyone tells you that classical music is dead you need just two words to refute them: Joe Hisaishi. The 75-year-old Japanese conductor, composer and pianist may be best known for his soundtracks, particularly his long association with Hayao Miyazaki’s Studio Ghibli films, but has parlayed his popular success into serious concert-hall credentials. You can debate style and genre, but there’s no arguing with the impact of a man who can sell out the Royal Albert Hall on a Monday night in November with an evening of music by Steve Reich, David Lang and Hisaishi himself – and not a film score in sight. articles.title: I don’t have children. A stranger decided I was ruining my life
articles.description: A reader sent me unsolicited photos of his children, insisting I was missing out on everything. Why are other people’s reproductive choices so threatening to many of us? Last fall, a man I had never met wrote to inform me that my fertility window was “rapidly closing” – and that I couldn’t possibly be happy. What had prompted this unsolicited assessment was an article I had published about how fascist regimes seek to control women’s roles in society. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It was a cover-up’: HarperCollins accused of using lawyers to shut down concerns about David Walliams
articles.description: Women who spoke to internal investigation about inappropriate behaviour by Walliams still too scared to speak out The publisher HarperCollins used a leading legal firm and a non-disclosure agreement to “cover up” David Walliams’ inappropriate behaviour towards women two years before the children’s author was unexpectedly dropped, according to former staff. Women had complained to the company’s management for years about the author’s alleged misconduct and harassment. The concerns raised included that Walliams had an “inappropriate” sexual relationship with a woman who was an intern when he first met her, had inappropriate interactions with at least three other women connected to the company including asking two for dates, and approached a girl who appeared to be in her teens at a book signing event. articles.author: Mark Hendricks
articles.title: Their loss changed Appalachian forests for ever. Now the American chestnut is back
articles.description: The trees have been functionally extinct in the US for nearly a century. But new techniques are creating plants resistant to the parasitic blight that almost wiped them out Jeff White is starstruck by a tree. The farmer and environmentalist from rural Maryland has an affinity with the American chestnut but has never seen one stretch from root to sky like this one. “About how tall is it?” he asks. “Over 70ft [21 metres],” says Cassie Stark, director of science implementation for the American Chestnut Foundation (TACF). “Just incredible,” White says, his gaze fixed upwards. “I’ve never seen one so tall and so healthy.” ‘Thompson’, above left, is an unusually tall specimen of an American chestnut, a now-rare species once ubiquitous in the US. Jeff White next to ‘Gladys’, a thriving 15-metre-tall pure American Chestnut in Virginia’s Lesesne forest Continue reading...
